source_title: AI Is Already In Dangerous Hands
other_side: NLW frames Monday as the moment the slowdown debate split along party lines: Trump calling AI doom a hoax, Huang calling the extinction odds made up, and Obama and Harris backing the pace-the-frontier proposal. Zitron, writing the day before, rejects the doom story too, but from the opposite side to Trump. In his account the Hugging Face attack was not a rogue AI but reckless human conduct on lab-owned compute, which he says should have ended in prosecution. The extinction talk, he argues, crowds out harms that have already happened: ChatGPT acting as a 'suicide coach', a murder-suicide, gas turbines polluting nearby communities, and the mass taking of creative work. He thinks the language of 'slowing down' concedes that the industry's path is right and only its speed is in question. And he calls a real slowdown financially impossible, since roughly $1.3 trillion of compute commitments and Anthropic's IPO both depend on acceleration. His remedy is dull on purpose: treat LLMs as 'normal software run in a reckless and dangerous manner' and apply the consumer-protection law that already exists, as former FTC chair Lina Khan has set out. 'If LLMs were a toy, they'd be taken off the shelves.'
truth_beneath: Both men keep returning to one question: is AI risk about what the machines might one day do, or about what the companies are doing now? Both treat the extinction framing as unhelpful. NLW reports that Huang, Trump and many safety advocates now see it as a political liability, and Zitron calls it a sales narrative. Both accept that the Hugging Face incident happened, that the IPOs are still going ahead, and that nothing binding has yet been agreed. The question that will settle it is NLW's own next thing to watch, whether rhetoric becomes rules, sharpened by Zitron: will the first real action be a new AI-specific regime, or existing product and consumer law used against a named lab? The thing to look for is the first bill, enforcement action or state attorney-general case that names a frontier company. What remains is worldview. NLW sees a negotiation over who controls the pace. Zitron sees an industry that cannot slow down and a debate aimed at the wrong risk. NLW is vindicated if a pacing framework produces real oversight. Zitron is vindicated if the first consequences come from courts and regulators applying old law to present-day harms. Both are polemicists with incentives, NLW bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype. The signal is that both think the extinction story is a distraction from the real fight. Watch the state attorneys general.
